prompt.context: Your client is Canoodle, a revolutionary mobile dating service which utilizes swipe technology allowing users to easily select mates based on their online profiles. Canoodle was started 2 years ago and now operates across the United States. Despite its success and mass popularity, Canoodle has remained unprofitable, and investors are starting to put pressure on the CEO, Stevie McDreamy, to turn the business around. McDreamy has come to you to help out Canoodle.
prompt.question: What should Canoodle do to become profitable?

clarifying_info.q: Does Canoodle operate outside the US?
clarifying_info.a: Canoodle only operates within the United States, with ambitions to expand internationally.
The app is free to download off all mobile application stores. Canoodle's main source of revenue so far has been through ad sales.
The company must show a profit within 2 years.
Canoodle is already an LGBT friendly dating app and caters to the sexual orientation of all its users.

The market for dating applications consists of approximately 4 major national competitors. Most users typically have 1-3 dating apps, and all 4 competitors have roughly the same number of users within the United States. Canoodle does not consider traditional online dating websites in the same market.

exhibits.title: Canoodle's Previous Performance
exhibits.shows: A chart showing three trend lines over 8 quarters (1Q FY2014 through 4Q FY2015): Revenue ($000s), User Base (000s), and Total Expenses ($000s).
exhibits.data: Revenue and User Base appear to grow initially then flatten or decline in later quarters; Total Expenses appear to stabilize. All values range approximately from 0 to 1,500 on the y-axis.

framework: Diagnose whether this is a revenue problem, a cost problem, or both — use Exhibit 1 to anchor the diagnosis
Identify new or expanded revenue streams beyond ad sales (brainstorm)
Evaluate feasibility and ROI of the most promising revenue initiative (premium tier)
Determine optimal launch strategy (city, timeline, breakeven analysis)

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1. What does it tell you about Canoodle's financial situation, and what type of problem is this?
questions.guidance: The candidate should observe that revenues have declined in line with slowing user base growth, while costs have stabilized. This is primarily a revenue problem, not a cost problem. Strong candidates will note that flat costs with falling revenue is a structural issue requiring a new revenue model.

questions.prompt: What are potential sources of new revenue for Canoodle?
questions.guidance: Candidates should brainstorm multiple categories. Strong answers include: (1) Selling user demographic data — though they should flag privacy risks; (2) Selling outside services such as emojis or stickers (in-app purchases); (3) Selling a premium subscription upgrade to users (CanoodlePremium); (4) Charging on the application store (download fee or in-app billing). Bonus credit for noting transaction costs, competitive response, or impact on current free users.

questions.prompt: McDreamy wants to pursue a premium service. Development costs are estimated at $500,000 and would take 6 months to build. What factors should McDreamy consider before committing to this investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should cover: Price point for the premium tier; Market size and addressable user base; Adoption rate among existing free users; Marketing spend required to drive adoption. Bonus points for raising: Customer churn / negative impact on current free user base; Transaction costs (app store fees); Implementation timeline and competitive response during the 6-month build period.

questions.prompt: McDreamy wants to launch CanoodlePremium in just one city first. Using Exhibit 2, which city should Canoodle launch in, given a target to break even within 6 months? The monthly price for the premium service is $3.
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate 6-month revenue for each city as: User Base (000s) x Adoption Rate x $3/month x 6 months. Then compare to the $500,000 development cost. Only Los Angeles exceeds the breakeven threshold.

math.setup: 6-month revenue = User Base (in users) x Adoption Rate x $3 x 6. Development cost to recover = $500,000.
steps: New York: 300,000 x 9% x $3 x 6 = $486,000 (does NOT break even)
Los Angeles: 350,000 x 8% x $3 x 6 = $504,000 (breaks even — exceeds $500,000)
Chicago: 200,000 x 10% x $3 x 6 = $360,000 (does NOT break even)
Houston: 175,000 x 9% x $3 x 6 = $283,500 (does NOT break even)
Washington D.C.: 230,000 x 7% x $3 x 6 = $289,800 (does NOT break even)
math.answer: Los Angeles is the only city where 6-month revenue ($504,000) exceeds the $500,000 development cost, making it the recommended launch city.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential new sources of revenue Canoodle could pursue beyond ad sales?

categories.name: Data Monetization
ideas: Sell anonymized user demographic data to third-party marketers
License aggregated behavioral insights to consumer research firms — note privacy risk

categories.name: In-App Purchases
ideas: Sell virtual goods such as emojis, stickers, or profile boosts
Offer one-time unlockable features (e.g., see who liked you)

categories.name: Subscription / Premium Tier
ideas: Tiered pricing with different feature sets

categories.name: Distribution / Platform Fees
ideas: Charge a download fee on app stores
Negotiate preferred placement or co-marketing deals with app stores

categories.name: Partnership & Services
ideas: Affiliate partnerships with date-night services (restaurants, events)
Cross-promote third-party services to matched users

recommendation: Canoodle should launch a premium subscription service (CanoodlePremium) at $3/month, beginning in Los Angeles, where projected 6-month revenue of $504,000 exceeds the $500,000 development cost and achieves breakeven within the required timeframe.
Following a successful LA pilot, Canoodle should evaluate national rollout based on observed adoption rates and user retention data.
risks: Sensitivity to adoption rate assumptions — a small decline in adoption in LA could push the city below breakeven
Risk of launching in a single city versus all at once (competitors could respond nationally while Canoodle is constrained)
Extra ongoing maintenance costs for the premium service tier could erode margins
Premium tier may cannibalize or alienate the existing free user base, reducing overall engagement and ad revenue
next_steps: Decide whether development will be in-house or contracted (time and cost implications)
Design and execute marketing campaign in LA to drive premium adoption
Define KPIs and a go/no-go threshold for national rollout
Monitor competitive response during the 6-month development and launch window
